network.overall_strategy: The network separates the two hardest problems in prebiotic arginine synthesis: building the five-carbon alpha-amino skeleton and installing the terminal guanidinium group. The primary branch follows the best-supported surface cyanosulfidic chemistry of Patel et al. to the experimentally characterized arginine alpha-aminonitrile, then completes free arginine by two plausible hydrolytic endpoints. A second branch uses ornithine as the immediate precursor and installs the guanidino group with cyanamide, because Orn-to-Arg chemistry is chemically short and conceptually strong. Ornithine is supplied by a low-selectivity but experimentally reported high-temperature CO/H2/NH3 catalytic route and by a deliberately speculative protometabolic alpha-ketoglutarate route. A lower-confidence cyanoacetylene detour is included as an alternative entry to the acrylonitrile hub. Contested direct Fischer-Tropsch-type free-arginine claims are not made a primary branch.

reactions.name: Cu(I)-mediated formation of acrylonitrile from HCN and acetylene

conditions.other: UV-compatible cyanide-rich surface pool or evaporitic shoreline; staged delivery of HCN and acetylene

reactions.mechanism: Cu(I)-mediated oxidative C-C coupling of cyanide-derived carbon with acetylene furnishes the C3 unsaturated nitrile.
reactions.reasoning: This is the best-supported entry to the arginine/proline C3 branch in the cyanosulfidic network of Patel et al. (2015). A surface setting is preferred because that chemistry relies on UV-compatible aqueous processing and local cyanide concentration rather than deep submarine conditions; alkaline-lake ferrocyanide storage offers a plausible cyanide reservoir (Toner and Catling, 2019), and early Earth surface UV remained available (Ranjan and Sasselov, 2017).

reactions.name: Alternative oxidative coupling to cyanoacetylene

conditions.other: UV-compatible cyanide-rich surface waters with staged reagent supply

reactions.mechanism: Cu(I)-mediated oxidative coupling of HCN-derived carbon with acetylene yields the more unsaturated nitrile cyanoacetylene.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) reported efficient HCN-acetylene oxidative coupling to cyanoacetylene in a related branch of the cyanosulfidic network. It is included here as an alternative entry node because it is experimentally accessible from the same feedstocks, although its downstream use for arginine is less directly demonstrated than the acrylonitrile branch.

reactions.name: Partial hydrogenation of cyanoacetylene to acrylonitrile

conditions.other: subaerial geothermal mineral interface or thin-film setting with episodic H2 exposure

reactions.mechanism: Heterogeneous partial hydrogenation reduces the alkyne of cyanoacetylene to the alkene, giving acrylonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: This exact cyanoacetylene-to-acrylonitrile step is speculative in the supplied arginine literature. It is included because Patel et al. (2015) make cyanoacetylene from the same feedstocks, and prebiotic H2/Ni reduction chemistry is at least chemically plausible in adjacent geochemical settings (Yoshino et al., 1971; Kaur et al., 2024). Selective partial hydrogenation, rather than over-reduction or polymerization, remains an unresolved risk.

reactions.name: Ammonia addition to acrylonitrile
reactions.mechanism: Aza-Michael addition of NH3 across the activated double bond of acrylonitrile forms beta-aminopropionitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) identified beta-aminopropionitrile as the key branch-point intermediate for arginine/proline chemistry. No specific mineral catalyst is required in the reported chemistry beyond access to ammonia in aqueous surface systems.

reactions.name: Photoreduction of beta-aminopropionitrile to beta-aminopropionaldehyde

conditions.other: UV irradiation with HS-/H2S photoredox; optional Cu photoredox acceleration; rapid downstream trapping favored

reactions.mechanism: H2S-driven UV photoreduction converts the nitrile branch-point to the corresponding aldehyde, beta-aminopropionaldehyde.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) specifically showed H2S/UV reduction of beta-aminopropionitrile to beta-aminopropionaldehyde, the stage at which cyanamide trapping becomes much more effective than direct aminonitrile guanidination. Surface UV availability is supported by Ranjan and Sasselov (2017), while sulfur availability is geochemically constrained and likely local rather than globally abundant (Ranjan et al., 2018).

reactions.name: Aldehyde-stage cyanosulfidic construction of arginine alpha-aminonitrile

conditions.other: UV irradiation; staged addition of cyanamide, HCN, H2S and NH3; optional Cu photoredox acceleration; flow or wet-dry cycling

reactions.mechanism: Cyanamide traps the aldehyde to a guanidinated aldehyde/hemiaminal manifold; HCN adds as cyanohydrin; H2S enables thioamide chemistry; repeated photoreduction and final NH3 addition furnish arginine alpha-aminonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: This is the strongest Arg-specific de novo branch. Patel et al. (2015) found aldehyde-stage capture by residual cyanamide to be markedly more effective than direct guanidination of beta-aminopropionitrile, and they structurally characterized the arginine alpha-aminonitrile precursor. The network is represented here as a collapsed multistep surface sequence because the published chemistry is staged rather than one-pot. Its geochemical plausibility depends on localized cyanide concentration and a workable sulfur/UV balance (Toner and Catling, 2019; Ranjan et al., 2018).

reactions.name: Direct beta-aminopropionitrile guanidination-homologation to arginine alpha-aminonitrile

conditions.other: UV irradiation; cyanamide present before photoreduction; staged HCN/H2S/NH3 inputs; optional Cu photoredox acceleration

reactions.mechanism: Beta-aminopropionitrile is first guanidinated by cyanamide, then carried through the same photoreductive homologation logic to the C5 arginine alpha-aminonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) reported direct cyanamide guanidination of beta-aminopropionitrile to be relatively inefficient, but not impossible. It is therefore included as a lower-efficiency alternative pathway. The later homologation to arginine alpha-aminonitrile is chemically inferred from the same cyanosulfidic logic, so this edge is less secure than the aldehyde-trapping route and should be treated as partially speculative.

reactions.name: Warm surface hydrolysis of arginine alpha-aminonitrile

conditions.other: wet-dry cycles or prolonged warm aqueous residence

reactions.mechanism: Stepwise nitrile hydration and hydrolysis converts the alpha-aminonitrile to the corresponding amino acid.
reactions.reasoning: Hydrolysis of alpha-aminonitriles to amino acids is the expected Strecker endpoint, so free arginine is the logical product of arginine alpha-aminonitrile hydrolysis. However, Patel et al. (2015) emphasized the aminonitrile precursor rather than a quantitative isolation of free arginine; this completion step is chemically expected but not directly established in the provided arginine literature and is therefore modestly speculative.

reactions.name: Compartmental aqueous hydrolysis of arginine alpha-aminonitrile

conditions.other: long residence in concentrated prebiotic pools or protocell-like compartments

reactions.mechanism: Slow aqueous nitrile hydration and hydrolysis proceeds under concentrated, retained conditions rather than open-surface dilution.
reactions.reasoning: This alternative endpoint keeps the final hydrolysis in a concentrated biochemical-style compartment rather than a surface wet-dry setting. The chemistry remains speculative because the supplied literature secures arginine alpha-aminonitrile more strongly than free arginine itself (Patel et al., 2015), but such compartmental retention is a plausible way to complete hydrolysis without assuming extreme temperatures.

reactions.name: Cyanamide guanidination of ornithine

conditions.other: concentrated pool or mineral interface; millimolar cyanamide; near-neutral to mildly alkaline pH

reactions.mechanism: The terminal delta-amine of ornithine attacks cyanamide, followed by proton transfers and tautomerization to generate the guanidino group of arginine.
reactions.reasoning: This is the shortest chemically credible late-stage route to arginine. Longo et al. (2020) demonstrated complete Orn-to-Arg conversion on model polypeptides in water and explicitly discussed cyanamide as a plausible simple guanidinating reagent; Steinman et al. (1964) supports cyanamide as a prebiotic reagent that can persist long enough to react. Late guanidination also helps avoid some ornithine dry-down liabilities noted by Frenkel-Pinter et al. (2019). The caveat is that a fully environmental free-ornithine plus cyanamide simulation to isolated arginine is still missing.

reactions.name: High-temperature catalytic synthesis of ornithine from CO, H2 and NH3

conditions.other: gas-solid catalytic interface with low overall selectivity

reactions.mechanism: Fischer-Tropsch-type surface reduction and coupling of CO with nitrogen incorporation from NH3 yields a complex amino-acid mixture containing ornithine.
reactions.reasoning: Yoshino et al. (1971) reported ornithine formation from CO/H2/NH3 over Ni, alumina or clay, and Hayatsu et al. (1971) subsequently confirmed ornithine by isotope/mass-spectrometric analysis. I therefore use this framework as an ornithine source rather than a secure direct arginine route, because ornithine was confirmed whereas arginine was not on the confirmed list. The pathway remains low-yield and mechanistically unresolved.

reactions.name: Net protometabolic conversion of alpha-ketoglutarate to ornithine

conditions.other: pH about 8; mineral-interface protometabolic chemistry; hidden glutamate-like intermediate not explicitly shown

reactions.mechanism: Net reductive amination first accesses glutamate-like chemistry and then, in a more speculative continuation, reduces and aminates the distal carboxyl functionality to the ornithine side chain.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) strongly supports the first part of this net transformation by showing H2/NH3/Ni conversion of alpha-ketoacids, including alpha-ketoglutarate, to glutamate under mild aqueous conditions. The continuation to ornithine has not been demonstrated and is explicitly identified as a major gap in the literature. This edge therefore deliberately departs from the literature by collapsing the supported alpha-ketoglutarate-to-glutamate step and the unresolved glutamate-to-ornithine bridge into one speculative net reaction for network compactness.

pathways.name: Direct acrylonitrile entry with aldehyde-stage trapping and surface hydrolysis
pathways.description: Highest-confidence Patel-style route in which acrylonitrile is formed directly, reduced to the aldehyde, trapped by cyanamide, elaborated to arginine alpha-aminonitrile, then hydrolyzed in warm surface waters.

pathways.name: Direct acrylonitrile entry with aldehyde-stage trapping and compartmental hydrolysis
pathways.description: Same Patel-style de novo branch as P1, but free arginine is completed by slower hydrolysis in a concentrated biochemical-style compartment.

pathways.name: Direct acrylonitrile entry with direct aminonitrile guanidination and surface hydrolysis
pathways.description: Lower-efficiency Patel alternative in which beta-aminopropionitrile is guanidinated before the homologation sequence, ending with surface hydrolysis.

pathways.name: Direct acrylonitrile entry with direct aminonitrile guanidination and compartmental hydrolysis
pathways.description: Same lower-efficiency direct-guanylation branch as P3, but completed by concentrated aqueous hydrolysis rather than open-surface hydrolysis.

pathways.name: Cyanoacetylene detour with aldehyde-stage trapping and surface hydrolysis
pathways.description: More speculative route in which HCN and acetylene first give cyanoacetylene, which is then partially hydrogenated to acrylonitrile before entering the stronger aldehyde-stage Patel branch.

pathways.name: Cyanoacetylene detour with aldehyde-stage trapping and compartmental hydrolysis
pathways.description: The same cyanoacetylene-entry route as P5, but finished by hydrolysis in a concentrated biochemical-style compartment.

pathways.name: Cyanoacetylene detour with direct aminonitrile guanidination and surface hydrolysis
pathways.description: Speculative cyanoacetylene-entry variant that bypasses the explicit aldehyde node and uses the weaker direct guanidination branch before surface hydrolysis.

pathways.name: Cyanoacetylene detour with direct aminonitrile guanidination and compartmental hydrolysis
pathways.description: The most speculative cyanosulfidic route in the graph: cyanoacetylene entry, direct beta-aminopropionitrile guanidination, then compartmental hydrolysis to free arginine.

pathways.name: High-temperature ornithine-first pathway
pathways.description: A heterogeneous CO/H2/NH3 catalytic route provides ornithine, which is then converted to arginine by cyanamide guanidination.

pathways.name: Protometabolic alpha-ketoglutarate ornithine-first pathway
pathways.description: A deliberately speculative protometabolic module converts alpha-ketoglutarate to ornithine under H2/NH3/Ni conditions, followed by cyanamide guanidination to arginine.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the best-aligned Patel-style branch conceptually: acrylonitrile formation, ammonia addition, aldehyde-stage cyanamide trapping, and aminonitrile hydrolysis are all literature-consistent ideas. But three key reactions are invalid as written. rxn_005 is unbalanced and needs explicit water input with NH3 and sulfur bookkeeping; rxn_006 collapses several Patel substeps and is missing one carbon equivalent, likely another HCN, plus unresolved O/S accounting; rxn_008 hydrolysis should consume 2 H2O and release NH3. As drawn, the branch supports arginine alpha-aminonitrile logic better than free arginine production.
suggestions: Split rxn_006 into the documented aldehyde trapping, cyanohydrin, thioamide, deoxygenation, second homologation, and final aminonitrile steps.
Rewrite rxn_005 with explicit H2O, NH3, and sulfur products/reactants under UV/H2S conditions.
Rewrite rxn_008 as aminonitrile hydrolysis with 2 H2O consumed and NH3 released.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Chemically this is similar to P1 and keeps the stronger aldehyde-stage Patel logic. The same stoichiometric problems remain in rxn_005 and rxn_006, and rxn_009 is also unbalanced: aminonitrile hydrolysis needs water as reactant and NH3 as coproduct. The move from a UV-driven surface system to a compartmental aqueous hydrolysis step is plausible, but the transfer mechanism and the 'Biochemical' environment label are underspecified.
suggestions: Keep the Patel branch but explicitly justify transfer from irradiated surface pools to a separate aqueous compartment.
Correct rxn_009 to include 2 H2O as reactants and NH3 as product.
Replace the generic Biochemical label with a geochemically explicit aqueous compartment description.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This shortcut is weaker than the aldehyde-stage branch. Literature specifically indicates direct cyanamide guanidination of beta-aminopropionitrile is relatively inefficient, whereas trapping the aldehyde is more effective. rxn_007 is also unbalanced, missing a carbon source and with inconsistent sulfur bookkeeping, so it cannot stand as a valid one-step guanidination-homologation. rxn_008 remains an invalid hydrolysis as written.
suggestions: Route through beta-aminopropionaldehyde instead of collapsing directly to rxn_007.
Add the missing homologation carbon equivalent, likely another HCN, and explicit intermediate nodes.
Correct rxn_008 stoichiometry with water consumption and NH3 release.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The conceptual Orn-free shortcut is attractive on paper, but it is not well supported by the cited Patel chemistry. rxn_007 is both mass-invalid and mechanistically overcompressed; the literature favors aldehyde-stage guanidination over direct aminonitrile guanidination. rxn_009 is a plausible endpoint type, but it is still unbalanced and needs explicit 2 H2O input and NH3 coproduct. Transfer into a separate compartment is not justified in the pathway description.
suggestions: Replace rxn_007 with multiple explicit Patel-derived substeps.
Correct rxn_009 stoichiometry and specify the compartment chemistry.
If retaining a compartment transfer, add a physical concentration/transport rationale.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Cyanoacetylene is a real literature branch point, but this detour adds uncertainty rather than solving any bottleneck. rxn_002 is unbalanced and likely needs H2 as coproduct; rxn_003 is plausible, but downstream validity problems remain unchanged. rxn_005, rxn_006, and rxn_008 all still violate conservation as written, so the pathway does not provide a valid route to free arginine.
suggestions: Correct rxn_002 by including the missing hydrogen coproduct and explicit oxidation context.
Only keep the cyanoacetylene detour if supported by a distinct environmental or yield advantage.
Fix the same Patel-branch balance problems identified for P1.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This route inherits the cyanoacetylene entry problem from rxn_002 and the same overcollapsed Patel chemistry downstream. rxn_009 is a conceptually reasonable hydrolysis setting but is still unbalanced and does not actually conserve atoms without added water and released ammonia. The surface-to-compartment progression is possible, but it is not physically specified.
suggestions: Correct rxn_002 and decide whether the detour is worth retaining at all.
Balance rxn_009 explicitly with 2 H2O consumed and NH3 produced.
Add a concrete transport/concentration step between the surface photochemistry and the aqueous compartment.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is among the weakest routes in the network. The cyanoacetylene entry already begins with an unbalanced rxn_002, and the key shortcut rxn_007 is both unbalanced and less favored by the literature than aldehyde-stage trapping. Final hydrolysis in rxn_008 is also invalid as written, so the route does not currently reach free arginine in a chemically valid way.
suggestions: Drop the direct aminonitrile guanidination shortcut unless it is rewritten as explicit low-yield substeps.
Fix rxn_002 with the missing H2 coproduct.
Correct the hydrolysis stoichiometry in rxn_008.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This combines two of the least secure decisions in the network: the unbalanced cyanoacetylene entry and the unbalanced, literature-disfavored direct aminonitrile guanidination shortcut. Although compartmental hydrolysis is conceptually acceptable, rxn_009 still fails conservation. The pathway is therefore not viable in its current form.
suggestions: Replace rxn_007 with the better-supported aldehyde-stage branch.
Specify a real geochemical compartment rather than the generic Biochemical label.
Correct rxn_009 with explicit water and ammonia stoichiometry.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the strongest target-achieving pathway in the network because rxn_010 is balanced and chemically plausible: ornithine to arginine by cyanamide guanidination is a strong late-stage concept. The weakness is rxn_011. The historical CO/H2/NH3 heterogeneous chemistry does not justify a clean single-step stoichiometric edge to ornithine; it is a low-yield catalytic product mixture, and the pathway omits the necessary catalyst/product-mixture context. A hot catalytic zone to aqueous guanidination transfer is plausible after cooling and collection, but it should be stated explicitly.
suggestions: Represent the CO/H2/NH3 chemistry as a low-selectivity catalytic source module or add explicit intermediates instead of a single ornithine step.
Specify catalyst/mineral identity and a cooling/collection step before rxn_010.
If ornithine-first is retained, support it with more direct free-ornithine plus cyanamide experimental framing.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The ornithine-to-arginine step is reasonable, but the upstream alpha-ketoglutarate claim is the weakest edge in the whole network. rxn_012 is unbalanced as written and overstates the literature: modern H2/Ni chemistry supports alpha-ketoglutarate to glutamate, not a direct nonenzymatic jump to ornithine. Even if rebalanced with extra NH3/H2 and H2O byproduct, the Glu to Orn bridge remains unresolved.
suggestions: Replace rxn_012 with the experimentally supported alpha-ketoglutarate to glutamate step.
Add explicit speculative Glu to Orn substeps rather than a single net conversion.
Use a geochemically explicit environment label instead of Biochemical.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network is topologically adequate and connected, and its strategy is literature-aware: it centers the Patel arginine alpha-aminonitrile module, includes the chemically strong ornithine-to-arginine guanidination idea, and does not overstate contested direct Fischer-Tropsch-type free-arginine claims. The main problem is validity and chemical specification. The deterministic check flags 8 of 12 reactions as unbalanced, including core target-forming steps. Specific fixes are needed: rxn_002 likely needs H2 as coproduct; rxn_005 needs H2O as reactant plus NH3 and sulfur outputs; rxn_006 and rxn_007 are missing at least one carbon equivalent, likely an additional HCN, and should be split into explicit Patel-style intermediates with proper O/S bookkeeping; rxn_008 and rxn_009 need 2 H2O reactants and NH3 coproduct for aminonitrile hydrolysis; rxn_011 should not be encoded as a single clean CO + H2 + NH3 -> ornithine step; rxn_012 overclaims the literature, which currently supports alpha-ketoglutarate only to glutamate under mild H2/Ni conditions. Environmental consistency is moderate rather than strong because the Patel chemistry needs explicit UV, Cu, sulfide, and staged aqueous conditions, while the Biochemical environment label is too vague and transfers between settings are mostly implied rather than justified. In its current form this is a connected, conceptually informed arginine network, but not yet a conservation-valid or fully chemically viable synthesis network.
